questions.statement: Which opening sentence states an opinion that the rest of the paragraph can defend?
questions.context: A student is writing an opinion paragraph for the school magazine and needs an opening sentence.

options.text: In my view, the school should start classes ten minutes later.
options.feedback: Correct. 'In my view' frames the sentence as a judgement, and the proposal it makes is narrow enough for a single paragraph to argue.

options.text: Classes at our school currently begin at seven forty-five.
options.feedback: This reports a verifiable time, so it is a fact and it commits the writer to nothing.

options.text: There are many reasons to think about the school timetable.
options.feedback: This promises reasons without taking a position, so the reader still does not know the writer's view.

options.text: Some students and other people disagree about starting times.
options.feedback: This reports that opinions exist in the community, which is not the same as stating one.

questions.explanation:
An opinion paragraph opens with a thesis: one clear position, marked by a frame such as in my view, that the rest of the paragraph supports.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence gives a reason that actually supports the opinion it follows?
questions.context: A student must justify a claim about school start times inside the same paragraph.

options.text: Later classes would help, because students who work night shifts need more sleep.
options.feedback: Correct. The reason names a group that the later start would genuinely benefit, so it explains the claim instead of repeating it.

options.text: Later classes would help, because a school is a place where students study.
options.feedback: This explains what a school is, which is true of every school and justifies nothing.

options.text: Later classes would help, which is what some students already say.
options.feedback: This reports who holds the opinion rather than giving a reason, so the claim is still unsupported.

options.text: Later classes would help, because later classes would help.
options.feedback: The clause restates the claim with different words, which is circular reasoning rather than support.

questions.explanation:
A supporting reason must connect the proposed change to a real consequence, such as an effect on sleep, time or cost, and not restate the claim.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence concedes the opposing point before disagreeing with it?
questions.context: A student is answering an article that argues the opposite of what the student thinks.

options.text: Admittedly the earlier start gives families more time in the morning, but it costs students an hour of sleep.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Admittedly' grants the opposing argument and 'but' turns the sentence back against it, which is a concession followed by a rebuttal.

options.text: The earlier start gives families more time, so the earlier start should stay.
options.feedback: This agrees with the opposing point and ends there, so nothing of the writer's own case survives.

options.text: The earlier start is often discussed, and the discussion is often long.
options.feedback: This describes how much the topic is discussed instead of taking any position on it.

options.text: The earlier start is not fair, and the earlier start is not popular.
options.feedback: Two flat assertions joined by and concede nothing and support nothing.

questions.explanation:
A concession uses a marker such as admittedly, although or while to grant the opposing point, and is then followed by a contrast that restores the writer's argument.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence offers evidence instead of a bare assertion?
questions.context: A student must support a claim about screen time without inventing data.

options.text: In our school survey of three hundred students, sixty per cent reported using a phone in bed.
options.feedback: Correct. It names a sample size, a method and a figure, so a reader can check the claim instead of taking it on trust.

options.text: Everyone knows that too many students use their phones at night.
options.feedback: 'Everyone knows' is not evidence, and the claim cannot be checked against any source.

options.text: Phone use at night is a very bad and really serious problem.
options.feedback: This stacks adjectives instead of data, so the strength of the feeling replaces the strength of the argument.

options.text: Phones have become more common in recent years than they used to be.
options.feedback: This may well be true, but no source or figure is offered, so it supports nothing on its own.

questions.explanation:
Evidence means a source, a sample, a figure or a named study. A strong opinion paragraph backs each reason with something the reader could check.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which revision makes the writer's opinion clearest without removing the support?
questions.context: A student has written a paragraph whose opinion is buried under hedges and is being reviewed by a classmate.

options.text: Replace 'perhaps it might possibly be argued that recycling helps' with 'recycling reduces the rubbish sent to landfill'.
options.feedback: Correct. The revision replaces a chain of hedges with a direct claim and leaves the topic of the claim intact.

options.text: Add three more hedges so the opinion sounds less strong to the reader.
options.feedback: More hedging weakens the position further, so the reader ends less sure of what the writer thinks.

options.text: Delete the opinion and leave only the facts about landfill figures.
options.feedback: Removing the opinion turns the paragraph into a report, which is a different genre from the one assigned.

options.text: Repeat the hedged sentence twice so the meaning becomes clearer.
options.feedback: Repeating an unclear sentence does not clarify it; the reader now has the same vague claim in duplicate.

questions.explanation:
Hedging markers such as perhaps, maybe and it might possibly be argued weaken a position. One clear claim plus its evidence is stronger than a claim buried in qualifiers.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: In a standard opinion paragraph, which sequence is the most logical?
questions.context: A student is planning the order of sentences in an opinion paragraph.

options.text: Thesis, reasons with evidence, a concession, and a restatement of the position.
options.feedback: Correct. The paragraph states its position, supports it, deals fairly with the other side and then closes by returning to its own claim.

options.text: A restatement of the position, the thesis, then a second restatement and finally the reasons.
options.feedback: This announces the conclusion before the argument exists, so the reader meets the claim three times and the evidence only at the end.

options.text: Reasons first, evidence last, and the thesis in the middle after the second reason.
options.feedback: Placing the thesis after the reasons leaves the opening sentences without a stated position to support.

options.text: The concession, then a summary of other essays, then the thesis, then one reason.
options.feedback: Opening with the opposing side and summarising other writers' work buries the writer's own claim and displaces the evidence.

questions.explanation:
The conventional order is thesis, support, counterargument and restatement, and moving the thesis later leaves the reader without a position to follow.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence is the strongest conclusion for this opinion paragraph?
questions.context: A student needs a closing sentence for a paragraph about public transport.

options.text: For these reasons, the council should add two evening buses before expanding the parking area.
options.feedback: Correct. It names the reasons with 'for these reasons' and returns to a concrete action the council can take, which closes the argument instead of repeating it.

options.text: The council should add two evening buses before expanding the parking area.
options.feedback: This repeats the recommendation from earlier in the paragraph without linking it back to the reasons given.

options.text: That is all I think about public transport for today, thank you for reading.
options.feedback: A sign-off in a paragraph is informal and adds no weight to the argument the paragraph has built.

options.text: In conclusion, this paragraph has been about buses and about parking areas.
options.feedback: The sentence names the topics rather than the outcome, so the reader learns what the paragraph covered but not what it argued.

questions.explanation:
A conclusion restates the position, ties it to the reasons already given and points to a concrete action, instead of merely naming the topic.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which paragraph represents the opposing view most fairly?
questions.context: A reviewer is checking whether a paragraph treats the reader fairly.

options.text: Some families rely on the early bus because no other service reaches their district, which is a real difficulty; even so, the current timings leave most students too short of sleep.
options.feedback: Correct. It states the opposing case accurately and then explains why the writer still disagrees, which is the difference between a concession and a caricature.

options.text: People who like the early bus obviously do not care about their own health.
options.feedback: It attributes bad motives to the opposing side instead of reporting its reasoning, which makes the paragraph unfair.

options.text: There is no serious argument in favour of the early bus, apart from the one just mentioned.
options.feedback: Calling the argument unserious dismisses it without engaging it, so the reader learns nothing about the other position.

options.text: The early bus is cheaper, cheaper and cheaper, and anyway nobody asked about it.
options.feedback: Repeating one point and adding that nobody asked replaces an argument with a dismissal of the audience.

questions.explanation:
Fair representation states the opposing argument in terms its holders would recognise, then disagrees with reasons. Attributing motives or belittling the view is not representation.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence states a requirement of an opinion paragraph rather than a preference?
questions.context: A student is deciding which sentence belongs in an opinion paragraph about remote work.

options.text: The writer must give at least one reason and one piece of evidence for the position taken.
options.feedback: Correct. This describes an obligation on the writer that can be checked, whereas a preference describes only what someone happens to enjoy.

options.text: The writer must use a pen rather than a keyboard when drafting a paragraph.
options.feedback: Nothing about drafting a paragraph requires a pen; this is an invented rule with no basis in the genre.

options.text: The writer must begin every paragraph with the word 'however'.
options.feedback: No single word is required at the start, so this states a convention that does not exist.

options.text: The writer must finish the paragraph within exactly forty words.
options.feedback: A word limit of forty is imposed by no rule of the task and is not a requirement of opinion paragraphs.

questions.explanation:
A requirement states what the writer must do, such as supplying a reason and evidence. A preference states only what someone likes and cannot be verified.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence would strengthen this argument the most?
questions.context: A student's argument about school uniforms rests on a single claim that has never been tested.

options.text: A comparison of attendance records at two schools, one with uniforms and one without, showed no measurable difference.
options.feedback: Correct. It introduces a real comparison with data, so a reader can weigh the claim instead of taking it on the writer's word.

options.text: It is obvious that uniforms stop every kind of bullying in every school.
options.feedback: The absolute quantifiers claim more than any evidence could support, so a reader is right to doubt the sentence.

options.text: Everyone in my family has always thought that uniforms look very smart.
options.feedback: One family's experience is not evidence about schools in general, however sincere it is.

options.text: Some people say uniforms reduce bullying, which is what the newspapers report.
options.feedback: This names unnamed sources without figures or findings, so the claim stays untested.

questions.explanation:
An argument is strengthened by evidence a reader could check, such as comparable data. Repeating the claim with louder words or an unnamed authority does not add support.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence best explains what is wrong with this paragraph?
questions.context: A student wrote: 'School uniforms should be abolished, because everyone agrees they are unfair.'

options.text: The reason offers no evidence and 'everyone agrees' hides who, if anyone, actually holds that view.
options.feedback: Correct. It names both faults: an unsupported reason and an appeal to an unnamed majority that the writer has not checked.

options.text: The paragraph is too short to be accepted, and no paragraph should be longer than one sentence.
options.feedback: No rule sets a length here; the defect lies in the reasoning rather than in the number of sentences.

options.text: The opinion is expressed in the passive voice, which is never allowed in an opinion paragraph.
options.feedback: The opinion is stated in the active voice, and there is no such ban on the passive in this genre.

options.text: The word 'abolished' is informal, and the topic of uniforms cannot appear in an opinion paragraph.
options.feedback: Abolish is a standard formal word, and uniforms are entirely suited to an opinion paragraph.

questions.explanation:
A weak reason and an appeal to an unnamed majority are the two commonest faults in an opinion paragraph, because neither can be checked by the reader.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence avoids presenting a personal preference as a general truth?
questions.context: A student must avoid turning a personal preference into a claim about everyone.

options.text: I find long classes tiring, although some students prefer two shorter periods.
options.feedback: Correct. The first clause limits the claim to the writer's own experience and the second clause notes that other students differ.

options.text: Long classes tire everybody, and no student anywhere prefers two short periods.
options.feedback: It generalises the writer's feeling to everybody and denies the experience of others without any evidence.

options.text: I find long classes tiring, so the timetable must be changed for the whole school.
options.feedback: The personal feeling is fine, but drawing a school-wide conclusion from it repeats the same generalisation.

options.text: Only my classmates and I dislike long classes, so nobody else in the country does.
options.feedback: Restricting the claim to one class and then excluding everyone else is an unsupported claim about the whole country.

questions.explanation:
A personal opinion is written in the first person and is bounded by the writer's own experience. Turning it into a statement about everybody needs evidence.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which modal best expresses a recommendation in an opinion paragraph?
questions.context: A student is writing about a proposal and needs the right modal verb for a recommendation.

options.text: The library should extend its opening hours so that students can study after class.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Should' presents the action as advisable and the clause after 'so that' supplies the reason.

options.text: The library extended its opening hours last September.
options.feedback: The past simple reports what happened and recommends nothing at all.

options.text: The library might have extended its opening hours last September.
options.feedback: This is a speculation about the past, which neither reports nor recommends anything.

options.text: The library would have extended its opening hours if the council had agreed.
options.feedback: This describes an unreal past situation and carries no recommendation about the present.

questions.explanation:
Recommendations take should or ought to followed by a base form. The other tenses and modals report or speculate instead of proposing.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence most honestly reports a limitation of this claim?
questions.context: A paragraph about online learning argues that screens are always harmful.

options.text: Studies of adult learners show that screen time alone does not predict results, so the claim is too broad.
options.feedback: Correct. It cites the limits of what the evidence shows, so the reader can judge how far the argument can be pushed.

options.text: Any study that disagrees with this paragraph must have been paid to lie about screens.
options.feedback: It answers contrary findings with an accusation instead of addressing them, which weakens the argument.

options.text: The paragraph is long enough, and only long paragraphs can ever be convincing.
options.feedback: Length is not evidence, and the claim about paragraph length is not a limitation of the argument itself.

options.text: Screens have been discussed for many years, and that is the whole of the matter.
options.feedback: Saying a topic has been discussed reports no limitation of the claim and closes the question without answering it.

questions.explanation:
Acknowledging what the evidence cannot show is part of an honest argument; dismissing contrary studies or invoking length replaces evidence with rhetoric.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence uses an example correctly as support?
questions.context: A student must support an opinion about cafeteria food with a specific example.

options.text: The salad bar is cheaper than the sandwich counter; for two dollars a student can eat there every day.
options.feedback: Correct. The semicolon ties one case with figures to the claim, so the example demonstrates the price difference rather than merely repeating it.

options.text: The salad bar is cheaper, and the cafeteria has several counters.
options.feedback: The second clause adds a true but irrelevant detail, so nothing supports the claim about price.

options.text: For example, prices in cafeterias are prices that cafeterias charge.
options.feedback: This restates the idea of a price instead of showing a real one, so no example is given.

options.text: The salad bar is cheaper for example purposes only in my own opinion.
options.feedback: The phrase for example purposes carries no example at all and the sentence ends on the writer's preference.

questions.explanation:
An example is a specific case with details a reader can picture or check. General talk about the category does not support the claim it is offered for.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence correctly attributes an opinion to a source?
questions.context: A student wants to describe one person's view without presenting it as true.

options.text: According to the school's head teacher, longer lessons would help every student.
options.feedback: Correct. 'According to' marks the claim as the teacher's judgement, so the writer's own voice stays separate from the position reported.

options.text: Longer lessons would help every student, as anyone can see.
options.feedback: This states the opinion as a general truth and adds an empty claim that it is self-evident.

options.text: Longer lessons help, and it is clear that the head teacher thinks so too.
options.feedback: The opinion is asserted first in the writer's voice, so the attribution does not frame it as someone else's view.

options.text: It is often said that longer lessons would help every student.
options.feedback: The vague passive 'it is often said' names no one, so the reader cannot judge whose opinion this is.

questions.explanation:
Attribution frames a claim as someone else's view, using expressions such as according to. A vague report that names no source cannot be weighed by the reader.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which connective correctly marks the reason that supports the opinion?
questions.context: A student must connect a reason to an opinion using the right connective.

options.text: Volunteering at the shelter is rewarding because the animals are cared for by students.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Because' introduces the reason that explains why the volunteering is rewarding.

options.text: Volunteering at the shelter is rewarding although the animals are cared for by students.
options.feedback: 'Although' introduces a concession, so the second clause works against the first rather than explaining it.

options.text: Volunteering at the shelter is rewarding but the animals are cared for by students.
options.feedback: 'But' signals contrast, so the reader expects the second clause to oppose the first.

options.text: Volunteering at the shelter is rewarding so the animals are cared for by students.
options.feedback: 'So' marks a result, which reverses the logical direction: the care of the animals is the result, not the reason.

questions.explanation:
Because introduces a reason, although and but introduce contrast, and so introduces a result. Mixing them up reverses the logic of the paragraph.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence mixes a verifiable fact with a judgement in one construction?
questions.context: A reviewer is checking whether a paragraph mixes fact with judgement in a confusing way.

options.text: The library opened two extra hours in March, which is a clearly unnecessary waste of money.
options.feedback: Correct. The first clause reports a verifiable change and the second adds the writer's judgement about it, so both appear in one sentence.

options.text: The library opened two extra hours in March because of the request from the students.
options.feedback: Both clauses report what happened and why, so this sentence contains no judgement from the writer.

options.text: Two extra hours in a week, added for some students in particular, is the kind of number that matters.
options.feedback: The vagueness here is a stylistic weakness, but there is no verifiable fact to report in the first place.

options.text: It would be better if the library added two extra hours instead of only one.
options.feedback: This is a single conditional proposal and makes no report of anything that has already happened.

questions.explanation:
Reporting a verifiable fact and attaching a judgement to it in the same sentence is a common slip; separating the report from the opinion keeps both clear.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence shows this writer reversing an earlier position, and what makes it a reversal?
questions.context: A student's paragraph claims that a policy works because it was introduced recently.

options.text: I used to argue that the policy was pointless; the attendance figures now show that it was working.
options.feedback: Correct. The contrast between 'used to argue' and 'now show' marks a change of position, and the evidence is named as the reason for it.

options.text: The policy was pointless, although the attendance figures show that it was working.
options.feedback: Although reports an objection the writer anticipates, not a change in what the writer believed.

options.text: The policy is pointless, and the attendance figures show that it was working.
options.feedback: Two opposing claims sit side by side without any signal that the writer has abandoned one of them.

options.text: The policy was pointless; the attendance figures show that it was working, and both are matters of fact.
options.feedback: Both claims are treated as equally valid facts, so nothing indicates a reversal of the writer's position.

questions.explanation:
A reversal is signalled by a change marker such as used to or I now believe, together with the reason that produced the change.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence best belongs in the strong paragraph rather than the weak one?
questions.context: A teacher is comparing a strong opinion paragraph with a weak one about the same topic.

options.text: Although the current timetable is cheaper to run, the cost of sleep for two hundred students is harder to defend.
options.feedback: Correct. It concedes the opposing cost, then argues the point on its own terms with a specific group affected, which is what the weak paragraph lacks.

options.text: The current timetable is very old and it is obviously a bad thing that some people like.
options.feedback: Calling the timetable old is a fact, but dismissing those who like it replaces argument with an insult.

options.text: Everyone knows the timetable must change, and anyone who disagrees is not paying attention.
options.feedback: An appeal to an unnamed majority plus an accusation replaces both evidence and fair representation.

options.text: Timetables, changes, schools and classes are all topics that people argue about.
options.feedback: Listing the topic's nouns adds nothing to the case and leaves the writer's own position unstated.

questions.explanation:
A strong paragraph states a position, concedes the opposing point fairly, argues with evidence and returns to its claim; weak paragraphs replace all of this with adjectives or generalities.
---
questions.subject: ingles
